questions.question: What is FRI primarily used to test in STARK-style proof systems?
options: That a large table of values is (close to) evaluations of a low-degree polynomial over a domain
That the prover knows a secret witness without revealing it (zero-knowledge) with no other assumptions
That a pairing equation holds for two elliptic-curve points (KZG-style verification)
That a hash function is collision-resistant by brute-force testing
questions.explanation: FRI is a low-degree test: it checks that an oracle/table behaves like evaluations of a bounded-degree polynomial.

questions.question: Why do many polynomial protocols pick a roots-of-unity domain of size n (power of two)?
options: It makes FFT/NTT-style structure available and makes pairings like x with -x easy to index
It guarantees soundness even if the verifier uses no randomness
It removes the need for commitments because the domain points are public
It forces the polynomial degree to be exactly n-1
questions.explanation: Roots-of-unity domains support fast transforms and structured pairings used by protocols like FRI.

questions.question: In this lesson’s folding step, how are two paired evaluations combined into one?
options: g[i] = (f[i] + β · f[i+n/2]) / 2  (mod p)
g[i] = f[i] · f[i+n/2]  (mod p)
g[i] = f[i] + f[i+n/2] with no dependence on β
g[i] = f[i] XOR f[i+n/2] treating values as bitstrings
questions.explanation: The fold is a linear combination with a random challenge β, scaled by 1/2 in the field.

questions.question: On a roots-of-unity domain D = {1, ω, …, ω^(n-1)} with ω^(n/2) = -1, which indices correspond to x and -x?
options: ω^i and ω^(i+n/2) because ω^(i+n/2) = ω^i · ω^(n/2) = -ω^i
ω^i and ω^(2i) because squaring negates a field element
ω^i and ω^(i+1) because consecutive powers differ by a sign
ω^i and ω^(n-i) because inversion is the same as negation
questions.explanation: The n/2 shift multiplies by ω^(n/2) = -1, giving the negated domain point.

questions.question: What is the main reason FRI needs commitments (e.g., Merkle) plus random queries in addition to folding math?
options: To stop the prover from changing earlier layers after seeing challenges and to force consistent openings
To compress the prover’s witness so it fits into a single field element with no interaction
To make the protocol work over any modulus including p = 2 without changing the folding formula
To eliminate the need for any randomness by making the transcript deterministic
questions.explanation: Soundness comes from binding the prover to layers (commit) and spot-checking consistency (queries).

questions.question: In the idealized degree-halving intuition of FRI, what happens to the degree bound after one folding round?
options: It roughly halves (degree in the new variable y = x² is about floor(deg/2))
It doubles because combining two points increases degree
It stays the same because folding is just reindexing
It becomes exactly n-1 regardless of the original degree
questions.explanation: Folding can be seen as producing a new polynomial in y = x², which reduces degree by about a factor of 2.

questions.question: Attack/soundness: what goes wrong if the prover can choose β after seeing which indices the verifier will query?
options: The prover may be able to craft answers that satisfy the queried checks while remaining inconsistent elsewhere
Nothing; β only affects performance, not soundness
It only reduces zero-knowledge but keeps soundness intact
It forces the verifier to read the entire table, but soundness is unchanged
questions.explanation: If challenges aren’t bound to the committed layers (or are chosen too late), the prover can adapt to the verifier’s checks.

questions.question: In the demo, flipping one evaluation changes the final folded value. Why doesn’t a real verifier just check the final value directly?
options: Because without commitment+query checks, a cheating prover could fabricate intermediate layers to reach any final value
Because the final value is always the same for all polynomials over a field
Because the final value reveals the witness and breaks zero-knowledge by itself
Because the verifier cannot compute the folding rounds without knowing the polynomial coefficients
questions.explanation: The verifier must enforce consistency between committed layers via openings; the final value alone is not binding.
